learning_goal: Know where each head of biceps and triceps starts and ends, and the exact bony landmark it uses.

structures.name: right scapula
structures.label: Scapula
structures.narration: The shoulder blade — origin of the long heads of both muscles.

structures.name: right humerus
structures.label: Humerus
structures.narration: The arm bone both muscles wrap around.

structures.name: right radius
structures.label: Radius
structures.narration: The biceps inserts here, on the radial tuberosity.

structures.name: right ulna
structures.label: Ulna
structures.narration: The triceps inserts here, on the olecranon.

structures.name: long head of right biceps brachii
structures.label: Biceps — long head
structures.narration: From the supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, running in the bicipital groove.

structures.name: short head of right biceps brachii
structures.label: Biceps — short head
structures.narration: From the coracoid process, alongside coracobrachialis.

structures.name: long head of right triceps brachii
structures.label: Triceps — long head
structures.narration: The only head crossing the shoulder — from the infraglenoid tubercle.

structures.name: lateral head of right triceps brachii
structures.label: Triceps — lateral head
structures.narration: From the humerus above the radial groove.

structures.name: medial head of right triceps brachii
structures.label: Triceps — medial head
structures.narration: The deep head below the radial groove — active in all extension.

structures.name: right coracobrachialis
structures.label: Coracobrachialis
structures.narration: The short head of biceps does not leave the coracoid alone: coracobrachialis leaves it with them, as a conjoint tendon. It is named twice in this scene, so it is drawn — the student can see which of the two muscles running down from the coracoid ends on the humerus and which carries on to the radius.

structures.label: Supraglenoid tubercle
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: CONTACT on FMA13395 (right scapula, 158.3 mm long axis z) against FMA37686, the long head of biceps — gap 0.55 mm, 1 witness. tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA13395 --contact FMA37686. Re-measured 2026-09-08: the previous coordinate was sound (1.04 mm away) but recorded a gap of 0 mm, which is not a measurement any surface pair produces.
structures.narration: The small bump just above the glenoid — where the long head of biceps begins.

structures.label: Intertubercular groove
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: nearest CONTACT point between the humerus and the long head of biceps (gap 0.39 mm); reproduced 2026-09-08 with tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA23130 --contact FMA37686 --slab z:0.75,1. Unified 2026-08-30 with gross__arm__humerus, which carries the measured value.
structures.narration: The gutter between the two tubercles — the tendon runs down it, held in by the transverse ligament.

structures.label: Radial tuberosity
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: CONTACT on FMA23464 (right radius, 229.4 mm) against FMA37686, the long head of biceps — gap 0.10 mm, 1 witness. tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA23464 --contact FMA37686. Unified 2026-09-08 with gross__forearm-hand__radius-ulna, which already carried this exact value while this scene sat 6.72 mm away. The short head (FMA37684) is NOT a valid second witness here — the two heads share one distal tendon but only the long head’s mesh reaches the tuberosity, and including it made the tool refuse at a 36.19 mm gap.
structures.narration: Where the biceps tendon attaches — pulling here supinates as well as flexes.

structures.label: Coracoid process
structures.calibrated_by: ONE LANDMARK, ONE PLACE. Unified 2026-09-08 with gross__pectoral-region-breast__clavicle and __pectoralis-minor, which carry this exact coordinate, were reviewed in the viewer on 2026-08-28, and rest on the better measurement: CONTACT on FMA13395 against all THREE structures that attach to the coracoid — FMA13375 pectoralis minor (gap 0.20 mm), FMA37665 coracobrachialis (0.16 mm) and FMA37684 short head of biceps (0.14 mm), 3 witnesses converging over 12.79 mm. Re-derived independently 2026-09-08 and reproduced to the digit. This scene had sat 6.87 mm away from its two siblings with a recorded gap of 0 mm. tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA13395 --contact FMA13375,FMA37665,FMA37684
structures.narration: The hook in front — origin of the short head, with coracobrachialis.

structures.label: Infraglenoid tubercle
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: CONTACT on FMA13395 against FMA37699, the long head of triceps — gap 0.61 mm, 1 witness. tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA13395 --contact FMA37699. Re-measured 2026-09-08: coordinate sound (0.47 mm away), recorded gap corrected from 0.1 mm.
structures.narration: Below the glenoid — the long head of triceps starts here, which is why it crosses the shoulder.

structures.label: Olecranon
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: EXTREME +z on FMA23467 (right ulna, 247.7 mm, long axis z) — the olecranon is the proximal tip of the ulna, a feature defined by POSITION, not by what touches it. 109.5 mm from the centroid, 1502 vertices considered. tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA23467 --extreme +z. Corrected 2026-09-08: this anchor had been defined as a contact against the triceps, which is wrong twice over — the triceps tendon attaches over a broad area (three heads converge with 15.43 mm spread, so no single contact point is the landmark), and the resulting coordinate sat 17.33 mm from the tip, the largest landmark error in the corpus. gross__forearm-hand__radius-ulna already carried the correct value.
structures.narration: The point of the elbow — all three heads of triceps end here.

views.title: See it in the body
views.narration: The biceps sits on the front of the arm, the triceps on the back — an antagonist pair moving the elbow.

views.title: On the bones
views.narration: They span from the scapula across the humerus to the radius — biceps — and the ulna — triceps.

views.title: Follow the long head
views.narration: Origin, course, insertion: it starts at the supraglenoid tubercle, runs down the intertubercular groove, and ends on the radial tuberosity.

views.title: What each one does when it shortens

ops.kind: shortening pulls the tuberosity forwards and round — flexion plus supination
shortening pulls the olecranon backwards — extension

views.narration: Watch the two ends of each muscle approach each other and the action names itself. Biceps pulls the radial tuberosity forwards and rotates it laterally, so it flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm — which is why it is strongest with the elbow bent, and why a corkscrew turns clockwise for a right-handed person. Triceps pulls the olecranon backwards and extends. The medial head does that in every extension; the long and lateral heads are recruited when the movement is resisted, and only the long head can also help extend and adduct the shoulder, because only it crosses the shoulder joint.

gaps: The transverse humeral ligament, which holds the long head's tendon in the intertubercular groove and is named in that landmark's narration, does not exist in the catalog — searched 2026-08-28 as 'transverse humeral', 'transverse ligament' and 'ligament'. Narration only; nothing on screen holds the tendon down.

There is no bicipital aponeurosis and no glenoid labrum in the catalog either, so the biceps' second, fascial insertion into the deep fascia of the forearm is not shown; the scene teaches only the tendinous insertion on the radial tuberosity.

Brachialis (FMA37668) and anconeus (FMA37705) are in the catalog and are deliberately NOT in this scene: the curriculum entry is biceps and triceps, and the flexor/extensor supporting cast belongs to the compartment scenes. This is a scope decision, not a missing mesh.

The six landmarks are measured, not placed: each is the nearest contact point between the bone and the muscle that attaches there (gaps 0.0–0.2 mm). Cross-checks on the scapula come out at textbook distances — supraglenoid to coracoid 24.1 mm, supraglenoid to infraglenoid 38.4 mm. They stay status:"needs-review" until a human has looked at them once.
